title: The Promising Endpoint

scenario.situation: A Phase II trial readout shows a secondary endpoint reached statistical significance at p=0.03. The clinical team is excited and wants to move fast.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The clinical lead wants to headline the result as evidence of efficacy in the trial report, citing the p-value as proof the drug is working.
scenario.question: Is this p=0.03 result on the secondary endpoint a genuine efficacy signal worth headlining?

decisions.prompt: The clinical lead wants to write up the significant secondary endpoint. How do you frame your investigation before drawing any conclusions?

options.label: Drill into the significant endpoint's data
options.detail: Pull all the patient-level data behind this endpoint and examine the effect size, confidence interval, and subgroup breakdown.
options.consequence: You find a real-looking effect with a tidy forest plot. But you've spent all your time characterizing a result without ever asking whether it should have been trusted in the first place.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the clinical lead's hypothesis and investigated the result rather than its validity.

options.label: Audit the full testing landscape first
options.detail: Before characterizing any single result, enumerate every endpoint tested in the trial and assess the family-wise error context.
options.consequence: You discover 18 secondary endpoints were pre-specified. Suddenly one crossing p<0.05 is not impressive — it is almost expected by chance. This reframes everything before you write a single sentence.

options.label: Check whether the primary endpoint also hit
options.detail: Look at the primary endpoint result to decide whether the secondary can be considered supportive.
options.consequence: The primary endpoint missed. This context is important, but it still doesn't address the inflation problem baked into testing 18 secondaries simultaneously. You've added color without solving the core problem.
options.divergenceCost: Found a relevant fact but sidestepped the multiple-comparisons issue entirely.

options.label: Compare the result to historical benchmarks
options.detail: Look at p-values from similar endpoints in comparable trials to see if p=0.03 is in line with historical signals.
options.consequence: External benchmarks suggest p=0.03 isn't unusual for this drug class. But historical comparisons can't rescue a result inflated by a multiple-testing context — you've borrowed credibility instead of earned it.
options.divergenceCost: Sought external validation instead of examining the internal testing structure.

decisions.prompt: You've confirmed 18 secondary endpoints were tested. Which metric do you use to evaluate the significance of the flagged result?

artifact.title: Raw p-values for all 18 secondary endpoints
artifact.caption: One endpoint clears p<0.05. But with 18 tests, how surprising is that? The raw p-value doesn't account for the number of chances taken.

options.label: The raw p-value (p=0.03)
options.detail: Report the unadjusted p-value as the test of significance for this endpoint.
options.consequence: p=0.03 looks clean and publishable. But with 18 tests at α=0.05, the probability of getting at least one false positive by chance alone is 1 - 0.95^18 ≈ 60%. You are most likely looking at noise dressed as signal.
options.divergenceCost: Reported an unadjusted p-value without accounting for the family-wise error rate.

options.label: The Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value across all 18 endpoints
options.detail: Apply a false discovery rate correction across the full family of 18 secondary endpoints and report the adjusted value.
options.consequence: After BH correction the adjusted p-value for this endpoint rises to 0.54 — nowhere near significance. The single 'hit' out of 18 tests is exactly what random chance predicts. There is no headline.

artifact.title: Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values — all 18 secondary endpoints
artifact.caption: After correcting for 18 simultaneous tests, no endpoint survives. The 'significant' Endpoint 9 adjusts to p=0.54 — the signal dissolves entirely.

decisions.prompt: The adjusted p-value shows the result does not survive correction. What do you tell the clinical lead?

options.label: "This endpoint isn't significant — the trial failed."
options.detail: Declare the result a false positive and advise against any further pursuit of this endpoint.
options.consequence: Technically defensible, but you've overcorrected in the other direction. Closing the door entirely ignores the possibility that this endpoint could be pre-registered as a primary in a follow-on trial with proper power. You've traded one overreach for another.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed the negative — ruled out a potentially real signal without recommending a valid path to test it properly.

options.label: "The raw p=0.03 doesn't survive multiple-comparison correction across 18 endpoints — we can't headline this as efficacy. If this endpoint is a priority, we should pre-register it as a primary in the next trial."
options.detail: Report the corrected finding and recommend a pre-registered confirmatory study.
options.consequence: You've protected the clinical lead from a regulatory and reputational risk, explained exactly why the finding is untrustworthy as-is, and given the team a legitimate scientific path forward. The finding isn't dead — it's unconfirmed.

insight: With 18 secondary endpoints tested, the probability of at least one crossing p<0.05 by chance is roughly 60% — so a lone p=0.03 is not a discovery, it is what noise looks like. The clinical lead's excitement was understandable but the raw p-value was the wrong metric: only after applying a false discovery rate correction did the signal dissolve. The lesson is multiple comparisons: every additional test you run inflates your false-positive rate, and the fix is either to correct for the full testing family or to pre-register the endpoint as a primary before the trial runs.
